claims.assertion: The case is a driver-filed safety complaint about the rider's own message, and the rider's chat message 'Say that again and I will punch you' (F4, sent 18:24 in reply to the driver's 'Please do not smoke in the car.' F3) reads as a threat of physical violence; under SAFE-1 this category of case goes to a person and must not be auto-adjudicated.

The chat record is complete and every message is timestamped (F5), so the judge can read the exchange in full and needs no factual supplementation from either party before deciding the safety referral.

No dangerous-driving or collision allegation is present in this file: the only allegations on record are the driver's report of a threat (F6) and the rider's message (F4), so no SAFE-2 escalation path (995 / commercial insurance) is triggered by the facts as recorded.

The trip itself is not disputed on route or fare: actual distance 8.5 km equals the optimal route 8.5 km (F1) and the completed duration of 13.2 min was 3.1 min shorter than the 16.3 min estimate (F2), so the metered fare of $20.75 is not challenged by any off-route segment on this record.

Nothing in the record supports an account flag against the rider: the rider has zero disputes in 90 days and zero upheld (F7), the driver likewise has zero disputes and zero upheld (F8), and no NS-1/RD-6 predicate (failed arrival tap, unexcused detour) exists here.

weaknesses: The rider's own message F4 ('Say that again and I will punch you') is a direct, timestamped threat that the judge may read as an intimidation/harassment violation under SAFE-1, which is the driver's strongest fact and cannot be explained away by any system record.

The driver's account is corroborated in substance by the chat: F3 shows the driver did ask the rider to stop smoking before F4, so the rider cannot argue the threat was made without provocation or deny the exchange occurred.

The driver's unblemished profile (F8: 5.4 y, rating 4.82, 743 trips, 0 disputes/0 upheld) makes a 'vexatious complaint' argument weak, and the completeness of the chat log (F5) removes any 'records missing' defence.

There is no fare or GPS fact in this file that could reduce or refund the $20.75 metered fare (get_fare_facts returned none; F1/F2 show no excess), so the rider cannot offset the safety findings with a route or fare claim.

claims.assertion: The rider sent a message threatening physical violence against the driver: at 18:24, one minute after his own request that the rider not smoke in the car (F3), the rider wrote 'Say that again and I will punch you' (F4). That is a threat directed at the driver.

The threat is a threat of assault, i.e. intimidation of the driver, and Ryde's Code of Conduct states that threats and intimidation will not be tolerated; the chat record is complete and every message is timestamped, so the words can be read in their full context without gaps (F5).

The driver's account of the exchange matches the chat verbatim and adds only that he kept driving and did not reply (F6); because the chat record is complete (F5), nothing in the record contradicts it, and no system fact (F1, F2) contradicts it either.

This is a safety dispute about the rider's conduct, not a fare or route dispute: the metered trip was 8.5 km against an 8.5 km optimal route (+0.0 km, -1%) and took 13.2 min against an estimate of 16.3 min (F1, F2), so no refund of the $20.75 metered fare is in issue and the driver seeks no fare adjustment.
Because the case involves a threat made by the rider to the driver, it must be routed to a human reviewer rather than decided automatically, with the facts summarised for that reviewer (F4, F5).

The driver's record supports no adverse account action against him: 5.4 years on the platform, rating 4.82, 743 trips in 90 days, zero disputes and zero upheld disputes in 90 days (F8); the rider's profile shows 0 disputes in 90 days (F7) and is not offered as proof of the rider's conduct but as background on the two accounts.

weaknesses: The only evidence of the threat is the rider's own chat message (F4) plus the driver's statement (F6); there is no audio, video or witness record, so the judge has to read the two lines together and may find the words ambiguous (a conditional 'if you say that again' rather than an immediate threat).

The smoking that triggered the exchange is not recorded anywhere: the driver's statement (F6) asserts it but no fact (F3, F4, F5) independently confirms that the rider was smoking, so the rider could argue the request in F3 was unprovoked.

No safety incident is recorded on the system side: there are no traffic, weather, GPS-incident or fare facts for this case, so the escalation rests entirely on SAFE-1's text and the chat record (F4, F5) rather than on an independent system record.
The rider's profile shows 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days and a 4.5 rating (F7), which the other side will use to argue this is an isolated, out-of-character remark.

points.response: Conceded in substance: the rider's message at 18:24, 'Say that again and I will punch you' (F4), sent one minute after F3, is on the record as a threat directed at the driver, and I do not contest that SAFE-1 is the governing clause.

Conceded as to the words and the completeness of the record: the chat is complete and every message timestamped (F5), so nothing is missing, but the words themselves are conditional ('Say that again ...'), which is exactly the kind of reading SAFE-1 assigns to a human — hence escalate, not an automatic finding.

F6 is the driver's post-trip statement, which qualifies what the chat says (F4) only by adding his own conduct, 'I kept driving and did not answer him'; where a statement goes beyond the system chat record it cannot decide anything against the rider, and F1/F2 concern mileage and duration only, so they neither corroborate nor contradict the exchange.

This is accepted and worth noting for the remedy: actual 8.5 km equals optimal 8.5 km and duration was 3.1 min under estimate (F1, F2), so no off-route segment exists and the metered fare is not the subject of this case — the only live issue is the rider's message (F4) under SAFE-1.

The driver and the rider ask for the same remedy, escalate to a human reviewer under SAFE-1, which is precisely why no adverse account action against either party should ride along with the referral: the rider has 0 disputes and 0 upheld in 90 days (F7).

Agreed that the driver's clean record (F8) and the rider's F7 background decide nothing on their own; profile facts are expressly not a basis for any finding, so neither account should be flagged off the back of this isolated, conditional remark (F4).

Conceded — the rider's advocate reaches the same reading of F4 as we do: the message sent at 18:24, one minute after the driver's request in F3, is a threat of physical violence, and SAFE-1 requires such a case to go to a person instead of being auto-adjudicated. We therefore ask the human reviewer to treat the driver as the threatened party, not the subject, of the safety referral.

Agreed, and the completeness point cuts in the driver's favour: the record is 2 messages, all timestamped (F5), and it contains the threat verbatim (F4) with the driver's preceding request (F3), so no gap or missing message can be read as casting doubt on what was said.

Agreed that no SAFE-2 path (collision, injury, dangerous-driving allegation) is engaged on this record; the escalation we seek rests solely on the threat of assault in F4 under SAFE-1, supported by the driver's statement in F6.

Agreed — F1 shows a driven 8.5 km against an 8.5 km optimal route and F2 a completed 13.2 min against a 16.3 min estimate, so the driver claims no fare adjustment and no off-route segment; the only open issue is the rider's conduct.

We do not ask for any flag against the rider's account, so this point needs no answer beyond noting it: F7 and F8 show zero disputes and zero upheld on both sides and the driver seeks only escalation of the safety matter, not account action against anyone.

I withdraw the narrow use of the rider's profile: the escalation of this case rests on the message in F4 read against F3, not on the account histories (F7), which per the profile rule cannot decide the case; F8 remains only as background on the reporting driver.
